items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a farm seen as a system with inputs, processes and outputs”.
items.answer: Farming system
items.markingKey: Farming system: a farm seen as a system with inputs, processes and outputs. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between intensive and extensive farming.
items.answer: Intensive farming uses large inputs of labour or capital on a small area to get high yields per hectare; extensive farming uses low inputs over large areas, with lower yields per hectare.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how physical factors affect the type of farming in an area.
items.answer: Climate (temperature, rainfall, growing season), relief and slope, and soil fertility and drainage determine which crops can grow and whether machinery can be used.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each factor with explanation up to [3]

items.stem: Study your case study of a farming system (for example commercial arable farming in East Anglia, UK). Briefly describe the inputs, processes and outputs of the farming system.
items.answer: commercial arable farming in East Anglia, UK: Inputs: flat land, fertile loam soils, about 600 mm rain, sunny summers, capital, machinery, fertilisers, pesticides, few workers; processes: ploughing, drilling, spraying, combine harvesting, storage; outputs: wheat, barley, sugar beet and oilseed rape sold for profit; extensive commercial with high yields.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Physical and human inputs, processes, outputs, classification of the system. [4]

items.stem: Farm A grows 14 tonnes of wheat on 4 hectares without irrigation. Farm B grows 10 tonnes on 2 hectares using irrigation, high-yielding seeds and fertiliser. (a) Calculate the yield per hectare for each farm. (b) Suggest two problems Farm B might face from using these methods.
items.answer: (a) Farm A: 3.5 t/ha; Farm B: 5 t/ha (b) High costs and debt; fertiliser and pesticide pollution of water; salinisation from irrigation; lowering of the water table.
items.markingKey: (a) tonnes ÷ hectares [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: With reference to rice farming in the Ganges delta, Bangladesh, or another example of a farming system you have studied, describe the inputs, processes and outputs of the farming system.
items.answer: Model answer (rice farming in the Ganges delta, Bangladesh): Inputs: monsoon rain (over 2000 mm), high temperatures, flat alluvial soils renewed by floods, family labour, buffalo, seed; processes: ploughing, flooding paddy fields, transplanting seedlings by hand, weeding, harvesting; outputs: two or three rice crops a year, mostly eaten by the family, with some sold; intensive subsistence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Physical and human inputs, processes, outputs, classification of the system. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: A student writes: “Subsistence farmers never sell any of their produce.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Most produce is eaten by the family, but small surpluses are often sold at local markets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how human factors affect farming decisions.
items.answer: Access to markets and transport, capital for machinery and fertiliser, government subsidies and policies, land ownership, labour supply and technology.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Farm A grows 4 tonnes of potatoes on 2 hectares without irrigation. Farm C grows 10.5 tonnes on 1.5 hectares using irrigation, high-yielding seeds and fertiliser. Calculate the yield per hectare for each farm.
items.answer: Farm A: 2 t/ha; Farm C: 7 t/ha
items.markingKey: tonnes ÷ hectares [2]

items.answer: commercial arable farming in East Anglia, UK: Physical: flat land for machinery, fertile soils, dry sunny summers for ripening. Human: large farms, capital, government subsidies, good transport to markets and processing factories.

items.stem: Explain the natural causes of food shortages.
items.answer: Drought and unreliable rainfall; floods; pests such as locusts; crop diseases; soil erosion; tropical storms.

items.stem: Explain the human causes of food shortages.
items.answer: War and conflict disrupt farming and transport; poverty; rapid population growth; poor infrastructure and storage; growing cash crops for export instead of food; high food prices.

items.stem: Study your case study of a food shortage in a country or region (for example the Sahel (e.g. Niger)). Briefly evaluate attempts to reduce the food shortage.

items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Short-term aid and long-term solutions; strengths and limitations. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of a food shortage in a country or region (for example the Horn of Africa (Somalia and Ethiopia), 2020-2023). Briefly describe the impacts of the food shortage.

items.stem: “Increasing food production is the best way to solve food shortages.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: The Green Revolution greatly increased yields in Asia; irrigation and HYVs reduce dependence on rain. Against: Many shortages are caused by poverty, conflict, waste and poor distribution rather than lack of food. Reducing waste, improving storage, transport, incomes and peace may be more effective; higher production can harm the environment. Judgement: Higher production helps, but tackling poverty, conflict, waste and access to food is usually more important.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Explain why high-technology firms locate in science parks.
items.answer: Near universities for research links and graduates; attractive environment for skilled workers; good motorway and airport access; sharing of ideas and services with other firms (agglomeration).

items.stem: Explain how the factors affecting industrial location have changed over time.
items.answer: Early industry was tied to raw materials and power (coal); now transport, communications and electricity let footloose firms locate near markets, skilled labour and pleasant environments, or abroad where labour is cheap.

items.markingKey: (a) tonnes ÷ hectares [2] (b) (5 − 2.5) ÷ 2.5 × 100 [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a widespread, severe shortage of food causing hunger and death”.
items.answer: Famine
items.markingKey: Famine: a widespread, severe shortage of food causing hunger and death. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the Green Revolution. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Food aid is useful in emergencies but can harm local farmers if it continues for too long.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Advantages: much higher yields, more food, fewer famines (India became self-sufficient in grain). Disadvantages: costly seeds and fertiliser led to debt for poor farmers; pollution; falling water tables; loss of crop variety. (b) Correct. Free food can lower local prices and discourage farmers from producing.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each side up to [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: For the Sahel (e.g. Niger) or another example of a food shortage in a country or region, briefly evaluate attempts to reduce the food shortage.
items.answer: the Sahel (e.g. Niger): Food aid and cash transfers; farmer-managed natural regeneration of trees; zaï pits and stone lines to conserve water; drought-tolerant millet and sorghum; the Great Green Wall initiative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Short-term aid and long-term solutions; strengths and limitations. [4]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows the average daily calorie intake per person in four countries. Country P: 3 000 kcal. Country S: 2 500 kcal. Country T: 3 300 kcal. Country Q: 2 200 kcal. The recommended average intake is 2 300 kcal per person per day. Suggest why a national average may hide food insecurity.
items.answer: Richer people may eat much more than the poor; rural and conflict areas may have far less; seasonal shortages are hidden.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: “Increasing food production is the best way to solve food shortages.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: poverty; Green Revolution.
items.answer: For: The Green Revolution greatly increased yields in Asia; irrigation and HYVs reduce dependence on rain. Against: Many shortages are caused by poverty, conflict, waste and poor distribution rather than lack of food. Reducing waste, improving storage, transport, incomes and peace may be more effective; higher production can harm the environment. Judgement: Higher production helps, but tackling poverty, conflict, waste and access to food is usually more important.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “raw material”?
options: A natural material used to make a product, such as iron ore or timber.
An industry that uses advanced technology and research, such as computing and biotechnology.
An industry that is not tied to raw materials and can locate in many places, such as electronics.
A group of high-technology firms located near a university to share research and skilled workers.
items.answer: A natural material used to make a product, such as iron ore or timber.
items.markingKey: Raw material: a natural material used to make a product, such as iron ore or timber. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “All industries must be located near their raw materials.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Agglomeration can reduce costs for firms.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Footloose industries such as electronics can locate in many places; markets and labour are often more important. (b) Correct. Firms share suppliers, skilled labour, services and ideas.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A company wants to build a food-processing factory. Fig. 4.2 describes three possible sites. Site A: next to a motorway junction on the edge of a city, flat greenfield land, 10 km from a university. Site B: beside a deep-water port with rail links, on cheap reclaimed land far from housing. Site C: in the city centre on a small brownfield plot with narrow streets and high land values. Suggest how local people might react to the new factory.
items.answer: Support: new jobs and income, multiplier effect. Oppose: noise, traffic, pollution, loss of open land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each side [2]

items.stem: Study your case study of an industrial zone or high-technology industry (for example Cambridge Science Park, UK). Briefly describe the impacts of the industry on the local area.
items.answer: Cambridge Science Park, UK: Thousands of skilled jobs; a cluster of over 100 firms and spin-offs; high house prices and congestion in Cambridge; pressure to build on green belt land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Jobs, multiplier effect, congestion, housing, environment. [4]

items.stem: With reference to Bengaluru, India (information technology), or another example of an industrial zone or high-technology industry you have studied, describe the impacts of the industry on the local area.
items.answer: Model answer (Bengaluru, India (information technology)): Hundreds of thousands of IT jobs and firms such as Infosys and Wipro; a growing middle class; but traffic congestion, water shortages, rising house prices and growth of informal settlements.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Jobs, multiplier effect, congestion, housing, environment. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Tourism can help to protect wildlife by making it valuable.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Entry fees and jobs give an economic reason to conserve animals and habitats.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how tourism can be made more sustainable.
items.answer: Limit visitor numbers, use local guides and businesses, charge entry fees for conservation, educate visitors, use renewable energy and recycling, protect sensitive areas.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 4.3 shows international tourist arrivals (thousands) to a national park in East Africa: 2000: 208, 2005: 262, 2010: 310, 2015: 371, 2020: 102, 2023: 419. Tourists spend an average of US$800 each; about 60% of this leaves the country (leakage). Calculate the percentage change in arrivals from 2015 to 2020.

Fig. 4.3 shows international tourist arrivals (thousands) to a national park in East Africa: 2000: 250, 2005: 283, 2010: 376, 2015: 550, 2020: 117, 2023: 489. Tourists spend an average of US$400 each; about 70% of this leaves the country (leakage). (a) Describe the changes in arrivals shown in Fig. 4.3. (b) Calculate the percentage change in arrivals from 2015 to 2020. (c) Explain why leakage is high in many LIC destinations.
items.answer: (a) Steady growth from 250 000 in 2000 to 550 000 in 2015, a sharp fall to 117 000 in 2020, then recovery to 489 000 in 2023. (b) -78.7% (c) Hotels, airlines and tour companies are often foreign-owned; food, drink and equipment are imported; managers may be expatriates.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark growth; 1 mark fall; 1 mark data [3] (b) (117 − 550) ÷ 550 × 100 [2] (c) 1 mark each up to [2]
